text: The 1938 War of the Worlds broadcast did not cause a nationwide panic. A ratings poll of 5,000 homes that night found only about 2% listening; newspapers, losing ad money to radio, inflated scattered reports.

In 1835 the New York Sun ran six articles claiming the astronomer John Herschel had seen bison, unicorns and winged bat-people on the Moon. Herschel, observing from South Africa at the time, had nothing to do with it.
The World Association of Newspapers recognizes the Relation, printed in Strasbourg by Johann Carolus from 1605, as the world's first newspaper.

Sweden's Freedom of the Press Act of 1766 is often called the world's first law protecting press freedom. It also gave the public a right to read official documents, an early freedom-of-information law.
Told a treatment would save 200 of 600 people, 72% of subjects chose it. Told the same treatment meant 400 would die, 78% chose the risky alternative instead (Tversky and Kahneman, 1981).

In a 1985 Stanford study, pro-Israeli and pro-Arab students watched identical news coverage of the 1982 Beirut massacre. Each side judged it biased against them, a pattern now called the hostile media effect.

In 2003 Barbra Streisand sued to suppress an aerial photo of her Malibu home that had been downloaded six times, twice by her lawyers. The suit drew over 420,000 visits in a month and named the Streisand effect.

In 1957 James Vicary claimed that flashing 'Eat Popcorn' and 'Drink Coca-Cola' during a film raised snack sales. In 1962 he admitted it was a gimmick: the famous subliminal advertising study was fabricated.

'A lie can travel halfway around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes' is not Mark Twain's. Its ancestor is Jonathan Swift's 1710 line: 'Falsehood flies, and the Truth comes limping after it.'

The claim that the US created AIDS began as a Soviet disinformation operation, first planted in 1983 in an Indian newspaper, Patriot. In 1992 the head of Russia's foreign intelligence service admitted the KGB's role.
On Easter Sunday 1929, publicist Edward Bernays had young women light cigarettes in New York's Easter Parade, billing them as 'torches of freedom'. His client was the American Tobacco Company.
The Catholic Church's Index of Forbidden Books, first issued in 1559, listed works by Galileo, Descartes, Kant and Victor Hugo, among many others. It was abolished only in 1966.
After Soviet secret police chief Nikolai Yezhov fell from favor and was shot in 1940, he was retouched out of a photograph that showed him walking beside Stalin at the Moscow-Volga Canal.

The word 'propaganda' comes from the Catholic Church's Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith (de propaganda fide), founded by Pope Gregory XV in 1622. Its sinister political meaning came centuries later.
Marshall McLuhan's 1967 book The Medium Is the Massage was meant to say 'Message'. According to his estate, a typesetter's error produced 'Massage', and McLuhan told them to leave it alone.

"What Orwell feared were those who would ban books. What Huxley feared was that there would be no reason to ban a book, for there would be no one who wanted to read one." (Neil Postman, Amusing Ourselves to Death, 1985)

"The press may not be successful much of the time in telling people what to think, but it is stunningly successful in telling its readers what to think about." (Bernard Cohen, The Press and Foreign Policy, 1963)
On 2 November 1920, Pittsburgh station KDKA broadcast the Harding-Cox presidential election returns, an evening often counted as the birth of commercial radio broadcasting in the US.
On Good Friday, 18 April 1930, the BBC's evening news bulletin announced: 'There is no news.' Piano music filled the rest of the slot.
In 1833 Benjamin Day launched the New York Sun at one cent, a fraction of what most papers cost. Its low price relied on mass circulation and advertising, the model behind most later mass media.
For 33 years Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein kept the identity of their Watergate source 'Deep Throat' secret. In 2005 he revealed himself: Mark Felt, who had been the FBI's second-ranking official.
Before telegraph lines linked Brussels and Aachen, Paul Julius Reuter used homing pigeons to carry stock prices across the gap, beating the mail train. The business grew into the Reuters news agency.

In 1981 Janet Cooke of the Washington Post won a Pulitzer Prize for 'Jimmy's World', about an eight-year-old heroin addict. Jimmy did not exist; she resigned two days later and is the only winner to return the prize.
Gutenberg printed roughly 160 to 185 copies of his Bible in the mid-1450s, about three-quarters on paper and the rest on vellum. Forty-nine survive at least in substantial part.

In 1735 a New York jury acquitted printer John Peter Zenger of seditious libel after his lawyer argued that true statements could not be libel. The law of the day disagreed; the jury simply ignored it.

A 'stereotype' was a printing plate cast in metal to reproduce the same image over and over. Walter Lippmann gave the word its social meaning in Public Opinion (1922), writing of 'the pictures in our heads'.

For the 1917 'I Want YOU for U.S. Army' poster, James Montgomery Flagg gave Uncle Sam a modified version of his own face. More than four million copies were printed; the design borrowed from Britain's Kitchener poster.

Hearst's supposed telegram 'You furnish the pictures and I'll furnish the war' rests on one 1901 memoir by reporter James Creelman. No such telegram has been found, Hearst denied it, and historians doubt it was sent.

A 2018 study of about 126,000 story cascades on Twitter found falsehoods reached 1,500 people roughly six times faster than true stories. Removing bots did not change the result; people did the spreading.
Often called the first web banner ad, AT&T's 1994 banner on HotWired asked: 'Have you ever clicked your mouse right here? You will.' About 44% of those who saw it clicked.
